title: Cancer Clusters and Random Clumps
objective: After this level you can explain why clusters of cases appear by chance and how investigators check whether one is real.
summary: Cancer is common, so cases clump by chance. Investigators compare observed with expected cases; one, rare or unusual cancers are the signs. Few suspected clusters are confirmed.

cards.headline: Several neighbors on one street get cancer. Surely that can't be chance?
cards.body: Worries like this reach local and state health departments, and they check them. But random cases don't spread out evenly across a map. They clump. The job is telling a clump from a cause.

cards.headline: Random means clumpy
cards.body: A cancer cluster is more cancer cases than expected among people in one area over a set period. The catch: cancer is fairly common, so cases can seem to cluster even when nothing connects them. Scatter a handful of rice on a map and some grains land in little piles, for no reason at all.

cards.headline: Observed versus expected
cards.body: So investigators count. They compare the cases observed with the number expected, worked out from cancer rates in a larger population, adjusted for age. They look harder when the cases are one type of cancer, a rare type, or in an age group it doesn't usually strike. And they watch the boundary: drawing the area around the cases after spotting them can create a cluster out of nothing.

cards.fact: Of 567 suspected cancer increases checked, 72 were confirmed and 1 had a clear cause.
cards.context: That comes from a 2012 review of 428 investigations by US health agencies since 1990. Three of the confirmed increases were linked to a possible exposure. A clump is always worth checking, but most are never confirmed as real increases.

cards.headline: Clusters: checked
learned: A cluster is more cases than expected

options.label: Any street with two or more cases
options.rationale: It must be more cases than expected, not just several.

options.label: More cases than expected in one area over a set time
Cancer that spreads from person to person
options.rationale: Clusters are about counts in an area, not spread between people.

options.label: Several tumors in one person's body
options.rationale: A cluster is about many people in a place.

questions.explanation: A cluster is a greater than expected number of cases among people in a defined area over a set period.

questions.prompt: One suspected cluster is 12 cases of many different cancers across all ages. Another is 4 cases of one rare cancer in children. Which deserves the closer look?

options.label: The 12 mixed cancers, because there are more
options.rationale: Mixed common cancers are what chance clumps look like.

options.label: Neither: clusters are always chance
options.rationale: A few are real; that's why they're checked.

options.label: Both equally, since every case counts the same
options.rationale: One rare type in an unusual age group is a stronger signal.

questions.explanation: One type, a rare type, and an unusual age group are the signs that a cluster may have a common cause.

questions.prompt: Using Level 6's rates, a cancer usually strikes 50 per 100,000 people a year. About how many cases would investigators expect in a year in a town of 10,000?

options.label: About 50
options.rationale: That's per 100,000; the town is a tenth of that.

options.label: About 1
options.rationale: 10,000 is a tenth of 100,000, so a tenth of 50.

questions.explanation: 10,000 is a tenth of 100,000, so expect a tenth of 50: about 5 cases. Investigators compare the observed count with that.
